title: record publication is not a deletion barrier, and its rejection still releases protection
trigger: start a detached async operation from the completion callback. `AgentSession.dispose()` can therefore finish before `recordWriter()` has published anything; and injecting `ENOSPC` only into unfinished-writer-record publication leaves `writerRecord` holding a rejected promise. The abandoned-work completion branch catches it, then calls `dropWorkspaceLease()` anyway
how_found_quote: The test adds a real `session_shutdown` handler to the real SDK child and gates only the record's disk publication. ... At the **real 30-second grace**, `.catch(...).finally(dropWorkspaceLease)` repeats that unsafe decision. ... at **30,109.6 ms** the capture has run and the directory is gone before the late write, which gets `ENOENT`.

title: the new mint can repeat, and materialisation destroys the existing path instead of allocating another
trigger: the generator combines wall-clock milliseconds and a **22-bit process-local counter**, seeded from only 22 random bits ... If it repeats, `ensureIsolation` writes a new owner and clears the old workspace once it sees no lease/writer/retiring marker. A live old owner marker alone does not stop it.
measured: 3,518 independent real `Snowflake.Source` instances, asked for their first value at the same millisecond, yielded a duplicate between sources **1,641 and 3,517**.
how_found_quote: two fresh processes with identical controlled clock and entropy inputs use unmodified `Snowflake.next()` and unmodified materialisation. Both return the same path ... after killing and awaiting the actual capture owner, the actual surviving `reference-transaction` hook reads the replacement's `second-only` from that repeated path.

title: successful record clearing can be followed by a new record at grace, with nobody left to clear it
trigger: the grace timer is cancelled only after the actual lease release succeeds. If that release waits behind a real sandbox lock for 30 seconds, the grace calls `recordWriter()` against `undefined` and publishes a second record. The disposed session has already consumed its completion callbacks.
measured: Before grace the one record is successfully cleared; after grace there are **two marks, one clear**, and a live second record.
how_found_quote: The probe holds the real native sandbox lock, performs ordinary real SDK disposal, and observes the actual 30-second timer. It does not replace disposal or the timer.

title: the retained record can keep its own process alive after every handler has finished
trigger: the pending teardown waits for the record's process to die, while its watcher/poll keeps that very process alive; a normal Bun child program opens a real SDK session in a real registered sandbox, abandons a shutdown handler at two seconds, and lets it finish its actual write at 2.5 seconds
measured: the same plain program with a 10-ms shutdown handler exits naturally with code 0. With the 2.5-second handler it does not exit
how_found_quote: A normal Bun child program — **not** a child Bun test runner — opens a real SDK session in a real registered sandbox ... The test then kills and awaits that exact process; ordinary clear removes its sandbox.

title: the real native descriptor error does not take the new errno branch; the advertised recovery view still omits the holder
trigger: In a child limited to 256 descriptors, opening real `/dev/null` descriptors to exhaustion reproduces that native error. A narrow canonicalisation seam arranges the same real exhaustion **after** `realpath` succeeds, so cleanup reaches the real native lock boundary
measured: the supplied native binary produces `code:"GenericFailure"` with “Too many open files (os error 24)” in its message.
how_found_quote: Actual native exhaustion under `prlimit --nofile=256:256`: native error has `code:"GenericFailure"`, not `EMFILE`; cleanup immediately reports “another run has held it for 60s.”
